extracted.intended_audience: media reform advocates, researchers, journalists, and concerned members of the public
extracted.subtask_description: A curated directory of groups, articles, books, and resources about media reform, corporate media ownership, alternative media, public-interest policy, and monitoring/advocacy. The page collects organizations and materials useful for researching and campaigning on media concentration, bias, commercialism, and access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media ownership concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: How concentrated ownership is across news media (e.g., 1983: 50 corporations controlled the vast majority; later editions noted fewer than two dozen, then six, then five corporations controlling most U.S. media).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical counts and ownership charts (The Media Monopoly, The New Media Monopoly, The Big Ten chart, 'Who Owns What' from Columbia Journalism Review, Global Concentration: The Media Ownership Chart) to assess whether a small number of corporations control newspapers, magazines, TV/radio stations, books, records, movies, wire services and photo agencies. High concentration signals need for reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of funding and 'money behind the media'
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether ownership, foundations, institutes, PR firms, and other funders influencing media content are disclosed and traceable (e.g., 'Media Transparency: The Money Behind the Media', 'exposes the right-wing foundations and institutes that influence much of what ends up in the mass media').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate availability of directories and investigative resources (Media Transparency, SourceWatch, Center for Media & Democracy) that document funding, PR firms, and industry-friendly experts; lack of transparency is an indicator of undue influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercialism and PR/advertising influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which advertising, corporate commercialism, and public relations shape media content (resources listed include Adbusters, Center for Media & Democracy, PR Watch, 'Toxic Sludge is Good for You!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for signs of native advertising, PR-driven stories, undisclosed sponsorships, and pervasive commercial messaging. Use watchdog resources (Adbusters, Stay Free!, SPIN Project) to identify commercial capture and PR manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological bias and misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of systematic partisan or ideological slant and misinformation in coverage (e.g., Media Matters 'exposes conservative misinformation', OutFOXed documentary on right-wing bias, Inkywatch monitoring for bias and deception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess media outlets for recurring ideological framing, factual errors, selective sourcing, and organized disinformation. Use monitoring organizations (Media Matters, FAIR, Media Watch, OutFOXed) and content-analysis projects (Media Tenor) as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localism and community media access
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent of community-controlled/local media and opportunities for low-power and public-access broadcasting (e.g., Prometheus Radio Project, MicroRadio Implementation Project, Alliance for Community Media, Public, Educational & Governmental access channels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate availability of low-power FM licenses, community radio/fm projects, PEG channels, and local independent outlets. Strong local/community media indicates greater diversity of voices and less corporate centralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative journalism capacity and protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability and strength of investigative reporting resources and legal protections for reporters (e.g., Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, Center for Investigative Reporting, Investigative Reporters and Editors, First Amendment Handbook).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure presence of investigative organizations, training resources, and legal support; stronger investigative infrastructure improves accountability and public-interest reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of independent/alternative and progressive outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability and reach of independent, progressive, and alternative media outlets and publishers (lists include Democracy Now, Alternet, TruthOut, The Nation, Mother Jones, independent presses like AK Press, Beacon Press).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess diversity of editorial perspectives outside corporate media, including nonprofit outlets, independent publishers, and local alternative weeklies. Robust alternative media provide counter-narratives and investigative depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet openness, broadband access, and digital divide
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which the Internet is open and accessible, how broadband and filtering policies affect information access (e.g., Center For Democracy & Technology, Digital Divide Network, NoFilters.org, Project on Broadband/Open Access).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate policies and infrastructure affecting net neutrality, filters in libraries, broadband deployment, and open-access initiatives. Barriers to access exacerbate inequality in information availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy, legal advocacy and regulatory enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence and effectiveness of public-interest policy and legal efforts addressing media concentration and ownership rules (e.g., Media Access Project, Democratic Media Legal Project, Consumers Union testimony before the U.S. Senate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for active litigation, congressional testimony, regulatory petitions, and public campaigns to enforce or restore ownership limits and public-interest obligations; the presence of such advocacy indicates institutional pressure for reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watchdog monitoring and content analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic monitoring of media content for racism, sexism, violence, factual accuracy, and influence networks (e.g., Media Watch, Media Tenor, Media Channel's Issue Guides, Rocky Mountain Media Watch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use content-analysis tools, issue guides, and watchdog reports to evaluate whether media coverage meets standards for fairness, representation, and accuracy. Regular monitoring highlights structural problems and trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence and conflict-of-interest disclosure for experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether experts, think tanks, scientists and nonprofit spokespeople disclose ties to industry or corporate backers (e.g., Institute for Public Accuracy, Integrity in Science 'exposes scientists’ and non-profits’ ties to industry').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sourcing practices in news stories and whether expert affiliations and funding are disclosed; undisclosed conflicts erode trust and can skew reporting toward corporate interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for public broadcasting and equitable political airtime
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies and initiatives ensuring public broadcasting and reduced-cost airtime for political candidates (e.g., Citizens for Independent Public Broadcasting, Alliance for Better Campaigns seeking reduced cost air-time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the strength of public broadcasters, campaign-media access rules, and efforts to lower cost barriers for candidate communication; such measures promote a more democratic media environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of research, data, and historical accounts on media power
rubrics_metrics.description: Access to books, academic work, and compilations documenting the political economy of the media (e.g., Ben Bagdikian's The Media Monopoly/The New Media Monopoly, Robert McChesney's work, 'The Making of a Movement', 'Networks of Influence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scholarly and investigative sources to contextualize empirical claims about ownership, influence, and policy; strong documentation supports credible advocacy and reform proposals.
